Unit 4 Seminar – Part 1: demo of correlation and regression (Fuel Consumption)¶

Task: run each step of the demo notebook with FuelConsumption.csv and review it against last week's theory.

This is a completed copy; the original notebook is left unchanged. Changes to the original code:

  • File names now use the 4.Unit04 prefix. china_gdp.csv was missing and was downloaded from the IBM Skills Network course this demo is based on. It reproduces the demo's saved output exactly (same first rows, β₁ = 690.45, β₂ = 0.9972).
  • df.corr() → df.corr(numeric_only=True), because pandas 3 no longer skips text columns automatically.
  • np.random.seed(42) was added so the random train/test split gives the same result every time. The original had no seed, so its coefficients (39.80 / 122.89) differ slightly from the ones here.
  • Two bugs in the model-evaluation step were fixed, explained where they occur below.

Which of the above variables do you think will work best to explain a linear relation with CO2 emission?

Answer. FUELCONSUMPTION_COMB has the strongest and most linear relationship with CO2 emissions (see the value below). However, the scatter plot shows three separate straight lines rather than one. These are the fuel types: for every 1 L/100 km of fuel, petrol cars emit 23 g/km of CO2, diesel 27 and ethanol (E85) only 16, and this ratio is almost exactly constant within each fuel type. Adding fuel type to the model would make the fit almost perfect. ENGINESIZE is also strongly linear (r ≈ 0.87). CYLINDERS only takes a few values, so it is less suited to a simple linear fit.

Model evaluation¶

In [17]:
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
test_x=np.asanyarray(test[['ENGINESIZE']])
test_y=np.asanyarray(test[['CO2EMISSIONS']])
test_y_ = regr.predict(test_x)  # FIXED: was regr.predict(test_y)
In [18]:
# FIXED: r2_score arguments were reversed (was r2_score(test_y_, test_y))
print("Mean absolute error: %.2f" % np.mean(np.absolute(test_y_-test_y)))
print("Residual sum of squares (MSE): %.2f" % np.mean((test_y_-test_y)**2))
print("R2-score: %.2f" % r2_score(test_y, test_y_))

Mean absolute error: 22.58
Residual sum of squares (MSE): 851.05
R2-score: 0.78

Bug fix in the evaluation step¶

The original notebook had two mistakes here:

  1. regr.predict(test_y) passed the CO2 values into the model instead of the engine sizes (test_x). The model was asked "what is the emission of a car with a 250-litre engine?" That is why the original output showed a mean absolute error of 9,933 and R² = −18.82.
  2. r2_score(test_y_, test_y) had the arguments reversed. scikit-learn expects r2_score(y_true, y_pred), and R² is not symmetric.

The corrected results above show the model's real performance on the 20 % of cars it hasn't seen.

Extension – multiple linear regression¶

The Unit 4 content also covers multivariate models. The same train/test split is reused to compare engine size alone with engine size, cylinders and combined fuel consumption together.

In [19]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
features = ["ENGINESIZE", "CYLINDERS", "FUELCONSUMPTION_COMB"]
rows = []
for cols in [["ENGINESIZE"], ["FUELCONSUMPTION_COMB"], features]:
    m = linear_model.LinearRegression().fit(train[cols], train["CO2EMISSIONS"])
    pred = m.predict(test[cols])
    rows.append({"predictors": " + ".join(cols), "MAE": mean_absolute_error(test["CO2EMISSIONS"], pred),
                 "RMSE": mean_squared_error(test["CO2EMISSIONS"], pred) ** 0.5,
                 "R² (test)": r2_score(test["CO2EMISSIONS"], pred)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)

[<matplotlib.lines.Line2D at 0x11eab8ade50>]

Roughly looking look at the data visualisation, it appears that the logistic function could be a good representation for this very dataset. The logistic function has the property of starting with a slow growth, increasing growth in the middle, and then decreasing again at the end

Implement the logistic function¶

In [22]:
def sigmoid(x,Beta_1,Beta_2):
    y=1/(1+np.exp(-Beta_1*(x-Beta_2)))
    return y

Fit the logistic function on this dataset and estimate the relevant parameters¶

In [23]:
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
popt,pcov=curve_fit(sigmoid,xdata,ydata)
print("beta_1=%f,beta_2=%f"%(popt[0],popt[1]))

##
x=np.linspace(1960,2015,55)
x=x/max(x)
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
y=sigmoid(x,*popt)
plt.plot(xdata,ydata,'ro',label='data')
plt.plot(x,y,linewidth=3.0,label='fit')
plt.legend(loc='best')
plt.ylabel('GDP')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.show()

beta_1=690.451711,beta_2=0.997207

How good is the logistic fit?¶

In [24]:
pred_norm = sigmoid(xdata, *popt)
print("R² of the logistic fit: %.4f" % r2_score(ydata, pred_norm))
print("GDP in 2014: actual %.3e, fitted %.3e (US$)" % (y_data[-1], pred_norm[-1] * max(y_data)))

R² of the logistic fit: 0.9728
GDP in 2014: actual 1.035e+13, fitted 9.040e+12 (US$)

Findings – Part 1 demo (review against the Unit 3 theory)¶

Correlation (Demo 1)

  • All three candidate predictors are strongly and positively correlated with CO2: combined fuel consumption (r = 0.89), engine size (0.87) and cylinders (0.85).
  • MODELYEAR shows NaN in the correlation matrix because every car is from 2014. A variable that doesn't vary has a standard deviation of 0, so Pearson's r can't be calculated.
  • The predictors overlap heavily. Engine size and cylinders have r = 0.93, and city and combined fuel consumption have r = 0.996 (combined consumption is calculated from city and highway). As in Unit 3, these features carry almost the same information.
  • The fuel-consumption scatter plot splits into three straight lines by fuel type (petrol, diesel, ethanol). This shows why plotting matters: one correlation coefficient hides a structure that a categorical variable explains.

Regression (Demo 2)

  • On the training data, the simple model is CO2 ≈ 124.2 + 39.5 × engine size. Each extra litre of engine size adds about 40 g/km of CO2.
  • The original evaluation step was wrong. It predicted from test_y (the CO2 values) instead of test_x, and passed r2_score's arguments in reverse order. This produced a mean absolute error of 9,933 and R² = −18.82. After the fix, the model's real performance on unseen cars is MAE = 22.6 g/km, MSE = 851, R² = 0.78. Lesson: a result that looks absurd usually means a bug in the pipeline, not a bad model.
  • Multiple regression using engine size, cylinders and fuel consumption raises the test R² to 0.87 and lowers the MAE to 16.0 g/km. This is the multivariate model the Unit 4 content describes.
  • The split was originally random with no seed, so each run gave slightly different coefficients. Fixing the seed makes the result reproducible, which is good professional practice.

Non-linear regression (China GDP)

  • GDP from 1960 to 2014 follows an S-shaped (logistic) curve. After normalising both axes, the fit gives β₁ = 690.45 and β₂ = 0.9972, with R² = 0.97.
  • The logistic function used here has its ceiling fixed at 1, which is the 2014 maximum after normalisation. The model therefore assumes that growth levels off at the 2014 level, and it already underestimates 2014 by about 13 %. It describes the past well but shouldn't be used to forecast beyond the data.
